network_thesis.headline: Korea plans every journey on Naver. The water journeys are next.
network_thesis.body: Korea is a peninsula wrapped in water — a megacity river (the Han), beach-and-bay metros (Busan), marquee islands (Jeju), a national marine park (Hallyeohaesang), and international corridors to Japan. Naver is where those journeys begin: Naver Map is the country's #1 navigation app, Naver Booking is how Koreans reserve, and Naver Pay is how they pay. A Navier foiling tier gives Naver the journey it can't route today — the fast water crossing — discoverable in Map, reservable in Booking, paid in Pay.
network_thesis.how_to_read: Each card is a real, ready market. Start with Busan — the most renderable, ready pilot — or pick any cluster. Seoul / the Han River is the strategic hero. The phased sequence is our recommended path, not the only one.
network_thesis.coverage_note: The same Navier fleet that anchors our 4 proposed markets extends across every coastline Naver Map already routes — the water layer surfaces natively in the directions Koreans and visitors are already requesting.

partner_context.their_ambition: You are Naver — Korea's platform giant. Naver Map (27M monthly users) is the country's default way to plan a journey, Naver Booking is how it reserves, Naver Pay (~31M users) is how it pays, and your visitor push is making Naver Map the arrival app for inbound tourism.
partner_context.their_pressure: Maps, booking and payments are won — but mobility itself is monetized by others. Every taxi, train and bus routed in Naver Map earns someone else the fare. The one mobility surface still unclaimed, by anyone, is the water: the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju's islets — journeys Naver Map cannot route today at competitive speed.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier gives Naver a first-of-its-kind owned mobility surface: a software-defined foiling fleet whose routes surface natively in Naver Map directions, reserve through Naver Booking, and settle through Naver Pay — premium water mobility as a platform-owned offering, not another aggregated taxi.

hero.title: Naver × Navier — the journey layer Korea plans on, extended to water
hero.subtitle: Every Korean journey starts in Naver Map. The fast water crossing is the one leg it can't route yet.
hero.what_we_do_together: We launch a Naver-integrated foiling water tier across Korea's busiest water surfaces — the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju's islets and the Hallyeohaesang marine park. Navier brings the software-defined hydrofoiling fleet and the network playbook now proven in the Maldives; Naver brings discovery in Map, reservations in Booking, payment in Pay, and the inbound-visitor funnel. Together we make the water crossing a routable, bookable leg of every Korean journey.

why_now: Foiling lifts the hull clear of the water: faster, dramatically more efficient per passenger-mile, smooth and near-silent, hybrid-capable with no charging dependency, and autonomy-ready. A ~100-vessel network is already ramping in the Maldives, and Korea's water is wide open — Seoul's 2025 Hangang Bus launch was criticised as too slow, Busan's waterfront has no in-app tier, and Jeju's islet ferries are aging. The platform that routes every Korean journey is the natural front door.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop - roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists - the Han River piers, Busan's harbour, Jeju's ports and the marine-park terminals. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the Quanta-LR hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all for the cross-border legs.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces converge on Naver's map: the technology crossed from prototype to platform; a ~100-vessel network is ramping in the Maldives; and Korea's water surfaces — a slow new river bus, an un-monetized Busan bay, aging Jeju ferries — are ready to surface as a clean foiling tier inside the app every journey already starts in.

multimodal_fit: Naver already runs the hardest parts of demand: journey planning at national scale (Naver Map), reservations (Naver Booking), payments (Naver Pay) and identity. A foiling water tier slots straight in — water legs appear in Map directions beside the subway and the bus, one tap reserves the seat, Pay settles it, and the visitor funnel lands inbound tourists directly onto the network.

differentiation.why_navier: Software-defined and autonomy-ready — a fleet built like a platform, matching Naver's own instincts. A ~100-vessel at-scale network already proving the model in the Maldives, directly relevant to Korea's many-island, river-and-coast geography. For Naver specifically: an owned mobility surface rather than another aggregated one.

proof_points.claim: Naver Map is Korea's #1 navigation platform.
proof_points.evidence: 27.05M monthly active users at the latest record — the default journey planner for Koreans and the arrival app for inbound visitors.
proof_points.source: Mobile Index via Korea Times / Asia News Network (2026)

proof_points.claim: Naver owns the discovery-to-payment funnel.
proof_points.evidence: ~38.8M monthly users across Naver services (~75% of the population); Naver Pay ~31M users — Korea's most widely used mobile payment.

proof_points.claim: Korea's regulators are pulling marine fleets toward clean propulsion.
proof_points.evidence: Korea's national 'Toward Green Shipping by 2050' plan / 2030 Greenship-K strategy mandates eco-friendly conversion of public vessels and targets ~118 eco-friendly ships converted by 2030 on the path to net-zero domestic shipping by 2050 — a direct tailwind for a clean foiling tier.
proof_points.source: Korea Ministry of Oceans & Fisheries / Argus Media, 2023

proof_points.claim: Seoul's own river-transport push proves Han River demand — and the speed gap Navier fills.
proof_points.evidence: Seoul's ₩150B (~$105M) Hangang Bus launched in September 2025 and passed 300,000 cumulative riders within months, but drew divided reviews and was widely criticised as too slow to be real transport — exactly the fast-foiling-tier opening.
proof_points.source: Korea Times / Korea Herald / Straits Times, 2025–2026

objections.concern: Is the range enough across Korea's water?
objections.response: Korea's water splits cleanly into short hops and long line-hauls. The Han River commute (~11 nm), Busan's bay (~4 nm), Jeju's islets (~4–6 nm) and the Hallyeohaesang marine park (~12–30 nm) all sit well inside the Pioneer II / N35 70 nm all-electric envelope; the Busan↔Fukuoka (~110 nm) and Jeju↔Busan (~157 nm) line-hauls run on the Quanta-LR hybrid (700 nm, no charging infrastructure required).

objections.concern: Why succeed on the Han River where the Hangang Bus underwhelmed?
objections.response: The river bus is a slow conventional craft criticised as not-real-transport; a 30+ kt foiling tier is a different product entirely — a genuine cross-city commute, premium-priced and on demand in the Naver app Seoulites already use.

objections.concern: Korea's winters, monsoon and typhoon season cut operating days.
objections.response: Foils ride above the chop and software-defined routing flexes with conditions, so the fleet runs smooth on days conventional ferries cancel; demand concentrates in the long beach-and-islet seasons the fleet is sized for, while the cross-border and business line-hauls carry year-round flow.

objections.concern: Is the network model proven enough to commit to?
objections.response: A ~100-vessel, $100M, 3-year network is already ramping with JIH Global in the Maldives, and a second island-network anchor is signed with the WorldBridge Group in Cambodia — the same software-defined, autonomy-ready foiling model, directly relevant to Korea's river, coast and many-island geography.

phases.rationale: Start where the water demand is densest, most renderable and ready — Busan's beach-and-bay waterfront, with captive ferry demand and ready piers.
phases.narrative: Busan is the proof market: a scenic beach-and-bay shoreline with no in-app water tier. A small Pioneer II / N35 fleet on the Haeundae–Gwangalli–Marine City hops and the Geoje run shows Naver users a water layer that feels like the rest of the app.

phases.label: Phase 2 — Jeju + the cross-border line-haul
phases.rationale: Layer in Korea's marquee island-tourism market (Jeju islet hops + resort arrivals) and the marquee international corridor (Busan↔Fukuoka) the Quanta-LR hybrid was built for.
phases.narrative: Jeju turns the story to premium leisure — all-weather islet hops and resort arrivals — while the Busan↔Fukuoka Quanta-LR line-haul opens the cross-border flow inside an app travellers on both sides hold.

phases.label: Phase 3 — the south-coast marine park + the Han River
phases.rationale: Carry the network into the Hallyeohaesang marine-park island-hopping mesh and the Jeju↔mainland line-haul, and stand up the strategic Han River commute once the Seoul map node is built.
phases.narrative: The south coast is where the island mesh matters — Yeosu, Tongyeong and their marine-park islands — and the Han River is the strategic hero: a fast foiling commute that turns Seoul's slow river bus into real transport.

phases.label: Phase 4 — the whole Korean water map
phases.rationale: With the clusters proven, knit them into one national in-app water tier across Korea's coasts, river and cross-border corridors.
phases.narrative: The end state: Naver's foiling water tier across the Han River, Busan's bay, Jeju, the Hallyeohaesang marine park and the cross-border corridors to Japan — one app, Korea's water.

markets.label: Seoul — Han River + Incheon Bay
markets.anchor_note: STRATEGIC HERO MARKET. Map node + boarding now built: top node seoul-incheon-korea is placed on Incheon Bay water with intra-city Incheon/West-Sea routes. Han River intra-Seoul legs (Yeouido/Jamsil/Ttukseom) are riverine and sit inside the global land-mask, so they light via the Seoul-Incheon cluster spine rather than individual map arcs.
markets.summary: Seoul just launched the Hangang (Han River) Bus (2025) but it is widely criticised as slow and 'not real public transport' — precisely the gap a fast, silent foiling tier fills. The Han River is a 30+ km waterway through a 10M-person megacity, and Incheon's West Sea islands (Muuido, Yeongjong) sit on the doorstep. This is Naver's strategic hero water market — turning a slow river bus into a genuine cross-city commute and premium leisure tier, routed and booked through Naver.

hero.title: Naver × Navier — the Han River, made fast.
hero.subtitle: Turn Seoul's slow river bus into a genuine foiling commute and the Incheon islands into in-app day-trips — routed and booked through Naver.
hero.what_we_do_together: Naver brings Seoul's default journey planner and its booking-payment rails; Navier brings the silent zero-wake foiling fleet. Together we make the Han River a real cross-city commute and put the Incheon West Sea islands in-app.

partner_context.their_ambition: Naver Map is Seoul's default journey planner — and today it routes river crossings over bridges because the water is too slow.
partner_context.their_pressure: The launched Hangang Bus is slow and criticised as not-real-transport; Seoul road congestion is severe; and the river is under-used as a mobility surface.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: A foiling water tier on Naver: a fast Han River commute (Gimpo/Yeouido↔Jamsil↔Ttukseom) that appears in Map directions beside the subway, reserved and paid in one tap.

markets.why_now: Seoul launched the Hangang Bus in 2025 to wide criticism that it is too slow to be real transport — a clear opening for a fast, silent foiling tier that turns the river into a genuine commute and premium leisure product, booked in the app Seoulites already use, with Incheon's islands on the doorstep.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling flies clear of the water at 30+ kt — a genuine cross-city Han River commute the slow conventional river bus cannot deliver, ~10x more efficient, smooth and near-silent.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on the existing and new Han River piers (Yeouido, Jamsil, Ttukseom, Gimpo) and the Incheon terminals — Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; no new infrastructure.
why_navier_now.the_moment: The 2025 Hangang Bus launch created the opening by under-delivering on speed; a fast foiling tier is the structural upgrade, routed and booked through Naver.

markets.multimodal_fit: Naver Map already plans the whole journey across Seoul; the foiling pier becomes the water node on the Han River — Naver to Yeouido, foil up the river to Jamsil, Naver onward — a river layer in the multimodal map Naver already runs.

proof_points.evidence: Seoul journeys are planned on Naver Map at national-record scale — the funnel for a river commute tier is already open in every user's hand.

proof_points.claim: The Han River is a major under-used mobility surface.
proof_points.evidence: A 30+ km waterway through a 10M-person megacity, with the river bus the only scheduled service — no fast point-to-point tier.

objections.concern: The Han River has bridges, locks and seasonal ice / monsoon flow.
objections.response: Foils ride above the surface chop and software-defined routing flexes with flow and conditions; the Hangang Bus has already proven year-round river operability on the same corridor, and Navier simply makes it fast.

objections.concern: Why succeed where the river bus underwhelmed?
objections.response: The river bus is a slow conventional craft; a 30+ kt foiling tier is a different product — a genuine cross-city commute, premium-priced and on demand in Naver.

objections.concern: Seoul winters freeze parts of the river.
objections.response: Peak commute and leisure demand runs spring–autumn, which the pilot is sized for; the Incheon West Sea legs run year-round.

end_state.headline: The water layer of the platform Korea plans every journey on.
end_state.addressable_footprint: Every Korean water surface Naver Map already routes around — the Han River through 10M-person Seoul, Busan's beach-and-bay metro, Jeju's island-tourism coast, and the Hallyeohaesang marine park.

steady_state.vessels_at_scale: 410 foiling vessels at the national ceiling (162 committed across the phased build)
steady_state.platform_mix: Pioneer II / N35 for the river, bay and islet capillaries + Quanta-LR for the Jeju and cross-border line-hauls
steady_state.tam_framing: Jeju alone drew ~13.9M visitors in 2025, Seoul is a 10M-person megacity, and the Korea–Japan strait carries year-round business and tourism flow — all running today on slow river buses and aging ferries, a premium water-mobility surface no app has monetised.

end_state.narrative: Steady state is not a pilot count — it is the whole Korean water map. Busan proves the model, then Jeju and the cross-border line-haul, the Hallyeohaesang marine park, and the strategic Han River: 410 foiling vessels across four clusters, on 20+ corridors, booked entirely inside Naver — Pioneer II / N35 for the river, bay and islet capillaries and Quanta-LR for the long Jeju and Japan legs. The Maldives' ~100-vessel network is the unit; Korea is that model brought home to a peninsula wrapped in water — the water layer of the app Koreans already live in.

close.title: Korea's journeys start on Naver. Now the water ones can too.
close.body: Busan first, then Jeju, the south-coast marine park, and the strategic Han River — the water layer of the platform Korea plans on.

whose_money_legend.navier_transport_revenue: Fare the Navier boats collect. This is the corridor P&L (atom.py). SOM/SAM rungs are in this unit.
whose_money_legend.journey_gmv: Total spend on the whole island journey flowing through the super-app: transport + food + stays + experiences + ads + parcel/logistics. Gross, all merchants. TAM rung is in this unit.
whose_money_legend.platform_take: The partner's own commission revenue on journey_gmv. Derived line — this is the number that makes a super-app care, not the boat fare.

ladder_transitions.headline: Network matures: faster, more comfortable boats grow the market + leading-operator capture
ladder_transitions.basis: Two-lever step. (1) Faster, more comfortable boats grow the cross-water market (induced demand). (2) Leading-operator capture lifts share from 10% floor to 25% mature, network-wide.

ladder_transitions.headline: Lens shift: Navier captured share → total inducible marine-transfer wallet
ladder_transitions.basis: Unit change. Divide SAM (the captured share) by leading-operator capture rate to recover the full inducible water-transfer market — the marine-mobility TAM.

ladder_transitions.headline: Marine transfer → total journey wallet (food, stays, experiences, in-app ads)
ladder_transitions.basis: Journey-wallet step. Each $1 of marine-transfer spend unlocks ~$3 of broader journey GMV across merchants the partner monetizes.

ladder_transitions.headline: Naver platform take on Navier-carried journeys
ladder_transitions.basis: Platform-take step. Platform commission applied to the journey GMV routed through the Navier network (Navier-captured subset, not the full induced market).
